name: Cavitation (ultrasonic fat)

lead: Ultrasonic cavitation uses low-frequency ultrasound through a handheld probe to target fat under the skin without surgery. It is sold in clinics and as cheap home units, and some looksmaxxing posters use it to slim the face and chin.

The idea is that ultrasound creates bubbles that collapse near cells and damage fat cell membranes, which lab studies of cells and vessels document. A few small human trials are registered, mainly on abdominal fat in women, with no results summarised. Forum users are split between those reporting benefit and those reporting none.

paras: People use home devices as a DIY way to spot-reduce fat on the cheeks and under the chin, while clinics offer it for body areas in a series of sessions.

The sources reviewed do not report adverse events from cosmetic cavitation. Lab studies show cavitation can damage cells and small vessels, and device quality varies widely. Regulatory status varies by device and country.

angle.text: Forum users, especially for DIY face slimming, use cavitation devices hoping to burst fat cells and slim the cheeks, jaw or belly. Only small registered trials exist, and no cosmetic results were located for the home-use claim.

lead: Ultrasonic cavitation, also sold as "lipocavitation", is a non-invasive body-contouring treatment in which a handheld device applies low-frequency ultrasound to the skin over a fat deposit. Marketing and forum guides say the sound waves form tiny bubbles in the tissue that burst and break open fat cells, after which the body clears the contents, leaving a slimmer contour without surgery [1]. In appearance terms the aim is a slimmer waist, abdomen or thighs and, in looksmaxxing circles, a leaner face, jawline and chin with more visible bone structure.

Cavitation itself, the formation and collapse of gas bubbles in a liquid under ultrasound, is a well-studied physical phenomenon with medical uses such as kidney-stone lithotripsy, and laboratory work has examined how inertial cavitation affects cells and blood vessels in vitro [2][3][4][5]. Whether consumer or spa devices reproduce these effects in living subcutaneous fat at a cosmetically visible scale is a separate question. Small clinical studies exist, mostly in women, including a 2019 randomised trial of combined radiofrequency and cavitation with a low-calorie diet and a 2020 pilot study combining cavitation with fat freezing; several further trials are registered, with no results summarised in the registry entries [6][7][8].

In looksmaxxing communities the treatment is discussed mainly as an at-home method for "spot reducing" facial and submental fat using inexpensive devices, and some posters call it a non-surgical alternative to procedures such as fat dissolving injections or buccal fat removal. Some users report improvements; others describe it as ineffective or say clinic treatment is likelier to work [1][9][10][11].

paras: Cavitation devices apply low-frequency ultrasound through a coupling gel with a moving probe. Clinic machines and cheaper consumer units both carry the "cavitation" label and differ widely in power and design; no standardised specifications exist for either.

Forum users often describe combining a cavitation unit with radiofrequency [9][12]. Treatments are usually described as non-invasive and without downtime, and the practice is sometimes grouped with other non-invasive body contouring technologies such as fat freezing, radiofrequency, laser, focused ultrasound and high-intensity electromagnetic devices [13][8].

In physics, acoustic cavitation refers to bubbles that grow and collapse under alternating pressure. Wikipedia distinguishes low-intensity ultrasound, where microbubbles oscillate without fully collapsing, from high-intensity ultrasound, where bubbles grow and then collapse violently (inertial cavitation), producing shock waves and very high local pressures and temperatures [5]. Near a solid surface the bubble collapses asymmetrically and sends out a liquid jet [5].

The history of the phenomenon runs from Euler's 1754 speculation through Osborne Reynolds and Charles Parsons in the 1890s to Lord Rayleigh's 1917 mathematical model of bubble collapse [5]. Medical uses of controlled cavitation include shock-wave lithotripsy and research on non-thermal tissue fractionation and blood-brain-barrier opening [5].

Reviews describe collapse of bubbles as capable of mechanical, thermal and chemical effects on nearby cells, including transient membrane permeabilisation known as sonoporation [2][3]. Microscopy work has shown cavitating microbubbles can deform small blood vessels on microsecond timescales [4]. These studies used cell cultures or specialised experimental setups, often with microbubble agents, and are not trials of cosmetic fat reduction.

Proponents of the cosmetic use say the effect selectively ruptures adipocytes and that released lipid is cleared by the lymphatic system and liver [1]. One forum guide aims to explain the biophysical and cellular basis in detail and states that the pictured results are exaggerated [1]. No study among those reviewed directly demonstrates this sequence in people treated with consumer devices.

Ultrasound has a surgical history in fat removal. Wikipedia describes ultrasound-assisted liposuction, a form of liposuction used for fibrous areas, gynecomastia and secondary procedures; devices from the 1980s and 1990s were linked to tissue damage from excessive ultrasound exposure, and later pulsed-energy devices were designed to address this, with burns possible if the probe overheats [14][15].

External cavitation devices work from outside the skin and involve no incision, which is why they are marketed as non-invasive alternatives. Liposuction itself dates to the mid-1970s work of Arpad and Giorgio Fischer in Rome and to later tumescent techniques developed by Jeffrey Klein in the 1980s [14].

A 2019 randomised controlled trial in 50 overweight women compared radiofrequency plus ultrasound cavitation twice weekly for five weeks with a low-calorie diet against diet alone. Serum leptin fell in the treated group, abdominal and waist circumference decreased significantly in treated women, and weight fell in both groups without a significant difference between them [8].

A 2020 pilot study in 90 women aged 18 to 65 over eight weeks compared diet alone, fat freezing plus diet, and cavitation plus fat freezing plus diet. All groups improved; the combination reduced fat mass, weight, BMI and abdominal circumference more than diet alone but did not differ from fat freezing alone, and fat-free mass was unchanged [8].

A 2018 interventional study of focused ultrasound (not cavitation specifically) in 31 healthy women reported reduced fat-layer thickness on ultrasonography and, in one patient biopsied 24 hours after a session, disrupted adipocytes with collapsed membranes [8]. A 2021 randomised trial examined focused ultrasound cavitation with aerobic exercise on abdominal and intrahepatic fat in people with fatty liver disease [8].

A 2016 narrative review covering seven reviews and 66 original articles found that cryolipolysis, radiofrequency, low-level laser therapy and high-intensity focused ultrasound showed statistically significant effects, typically a mild to moderate circumference reduction of about 2 to 4 cm, and noted that differences in methods make device comparisons difficult [8]. A 2024 narrative review of 193 references organises evidence by device, with FDA-cleared devices, side effects and protocols covered in each section [8]. A PubMed search lists dozens of further reviews of non-invasive contouring [16].

For context, the Wikipedia article on cryolipolysis cites a 2023 review of 18 studies finding ultrasound-measured fat thickness reductions of 2.0 to 5.1 mm with that technology and describes data quality as low [13].

A small number of human trials are registered on ClinicalTrials.gov. They include a comparison of cavitation frequencies on abdominal adiposity in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (30 participants, completed) [6], a phase 2 trial of cavitation ultrasound in PCOS with 198 participants (completed) [7], a trial of cavitation versus electrolipolysis in obese infertile women with PCOS [17], a trial in adolescent females with abdominal obesity [18], and a trial of insulin resistance in women with central obesity that was recruiting at last listing [19]. Other registrations cover lipedema and postnatal women with diastasis recti [20][21].

These registrations list conditions such as obesity or PCOS rather than cosmetic facial contouring, and the registry entries do not report outcome results. No registered trial in these sources studies at-home facial cavitation devices.

A long looksmax.org guide presents ultrasonic cavitation as a way to reduce subcutaneous facial fat at home; its author notes that other users often dismiss the method, and the post carries a disclaimer that it is not medical advice [1]. A second guide, written to answer questions about a hollow-cheeks guide, lists risks the author associates with the method, including skin damage, burns, asymmetry, thyroid damage, hearing and vision harm [11].

Shorter threads show a range of views. One poster says it works but advises against using it on the face and says a clinic is likelier to give results; replies describe it as a hardmaxx and suggest considering it only at very low body-fat levels [10]. Other threads ask for ratings of specific devices, weigh a device against an injectable fat dissolver, and ask whether ultrasound is a non-surgical alternative to buccal fat removal [22][23][24].

In another thread a user starting cavitation with radiofrequency says it should work, a replying user says they tried it and recommends an injectable fat-dissolving product instead, and the original poster answers that the failed attempt may have involved a poor device [9]. An introductory thread describes combining ultrasound and radio frequencies as an affordable do-it-yourself route [12].

Laboratory cavitation research documents bubble-induced effects on cells and small vessels, and one forum guide lists burns, skin damage and asymmetry among risks [2][4][11]. Reviews of non-invasive contouring generally describe side effects device by device [8]. Surgical ultrasound-assisted liposuction has documented burn risk from overheating probes [14][15].

Device quality varies widely and consumer units have no standard specification. Regulatory status varies by device and country, and this article has not found a regulator page specific to home cavitation units.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, cavitation is discussed as a cheap, non-surgical facial slimming option, with posters split between those who report benefit, those who say it fails, and those who warn of risks [1][9][10][11].
